The viewer's buttons are the controls'. |
| Status colors | `--orbit-status-active`, `--orbit-status-done`, `--orbit-status-blocked`, `--orbit-status-todo`, `--orbit-status-neutral` |
| Error card | `--orbit-error-background`, `--orbit-error-border`, `--orbit-error-text` |

The list is also exported as `THEME_TOKENS`, and `themeTokens(name)` returns a theme's values, for example to style the rest of your page to match:

```ts
import { themeTokens } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

const night = themeTokens('night');
document.body.style.background = night.surface;
```

## Fonts

Maps draw with the reader's system font, unless the page gives them its own. Themes use fonts by kind: most draw in a sans-serif, `blueprint` in a monospaced font and `ink` its names in a serif. Give the page's font of each kind, and every theme draws with it in its own way:

```css
orbit-map,
.my-map {
  --orbit-sans-font: 'Google Sans Flex', system-ui, sans-serif;  /* every sans-serif theme, and ink's controls */
  --orbit-serif-font: 'Source Serif 4', Georgia, serif;          /* ink's names */
  --orbit-mono-font: 'JetBrains Mono', ui-monospace, monospace;  /* blueprint */
}
```

`--orbit-font-family` sets one map's font whatever its theme, and `--orbit-label-font` and `--orbit-display-font` only its names and the focused node's.

Names are measured in the font they're drawn in, so a name fills its node as far as it really reaches and never spills out of it, whatever the font, its weight or its letter spacing:

- **Lines** break at spaces, and inside long identifiers where they read, balanced so a name follows its node's round shape ("Lanzamiento / en México" rather than "Lanzamiento en / México").
- **Narrower widths:** with a font that has a width axis (Google Sans Flex, Roboto Flex, Roboto and others), a name that would otherwise be cut short is drawn semi-condensed or condensed when that shows it whole. Other fonts keep their width.
- **Web fonts:** names are fitted again when a font finishes loading, so a map drawn before its font arrives settles into it. The page doesn't need to wait for its fonts before drawing a map.
- **Exports** break names where the map shows them. Without a browser to measure in (`renderToSVGString` on a server), widths are estimated from the kind of each character.

## Shaping planets

Rims, shadows, the sun's halo, orbits and lines take the color of the node they belong to, mixed with a color of the theme. The `-tint` properties say how much of the node's color goes in: `--orbit-node-stroke-tint: 78%` draws the rim with 78% of the node's color and 22% of `--orbit-node-stroke`; `100%` is the node's color alone and `0%` the theme's color alone.

Widths are in screen pixels; `-offset` and `-size` are in node radii, so `--orbit-node-shadow-offset: 0.16` drops the shadow by about a sixth of the node's radius. Dashes take a `stroke-dasharray` (`4 4`, or `none` for a solid line).

```css
/* Flat planets with a dark outline and no shadow */
.roadmap {
  --orbit-node-highlight: transparent;
  --orbit-node-shading: transparent;
  --orbit-node-stroke: #1f2733;
  --orbit-node-stroke-tint: 0%;
  --orbit-node-stroke-width: 2;
  --orbit-node-shadow-opacity: 0;
  --orbit-sun-shadow-opacity: 0;
}

/* A glow in each planet's own color instead of a shadow */
.roadmap {
  --orbit-node-shadow-tint: 100%;
  --orbit-node-shadow-offset: 0;
  --orbit-node-shadow-size: 1.2;
  --orbit-node-shadow-opacity: 0.45;
}
```

The shading is one radial gradient over every node, from `--orbit-node-highlight` at its center through `--orbit-node-terminator` to `--orbit-node-shading` at its edge. `--orbit-node-shade-circle` places it: its center, then its radius, in fractions of the node's box. The default, `0.34 0.3 0.78`, lights spheres from the top left. A circle a little to the bottom right with bright outer colors makes glass instead, catching the light along the rim, as `liquid` does:

```css
/* Clear glass, with light along the rim */
.roadmap {
  --orbit-node-fill-opacity: 0.25;
  --orbit-node-highlight: transparent;
  --orbit-node-terminator: rgba(16, 24, 60, 0.07);
  --orbit-node-shading: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.95);
  --orbit-node-shade-circle: 0.53 0.55 0.56;
}
```

The circle is read when the theme is set, and is the same for every node of a map.

## Colors in code

```ts
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  theme: { preset: 'night', tokens: { surface: '#0b1020', 'font-family': 'Inter, sans-serif', 'ring-dash': 'none' } },
  palette: ['#ffd166', '#ef476f', '#06d6a0', '#118ab2'],
});
```

- `theme` takes a theme name or an object. The object's `preset` picks the theme to start from (without one, the document's theme or `paper`), and `tokens` sets any property by name, without the `--orbit-` prefix. Properties set in the page's CSS still win.
- `palette` replaces the node colors: the first for the root, then one per top-level branch, cycling when there are more branches than colors.
- A node's own `color` (`<!-- orbit color: #ef476f -->`, or `color:` in YAML) always wins.

## How nodes get their colors

Each top-level branch takes the next palette color, and everything under it uses shades of that color, mixed toward `--orbit-shade-light` or `--orbit-shade-dark` by position, so siblings stay distinguishable and a node keeps its color in every view. Labels use whichever of the theme's dark and light text has more contrast with the node, custom colors included.

## Dark mode

- `theme: 'auto'` follows the reader's system preference.
- To follow your site's own switch, set the theme when it changes: `renderer.setOptions({ theme: isDark ? 'night' : 'paper' })`, or update the `theme` attribute or prop.
- `night`, `glass-night`, `cosmos`, `blueprint`, `flat-night`, `material-night` and `liquid-night` are dark: they tell the browser so (`color-scheme: dark`), which darkens scrollbars and form controls in the detail sheet.
- Themes that paint their own background can let your page show through instead: set `--orbit-surface: transparent` and `--orbit-surface-pattern: none`.

## Exports

`renderToSVGString(markdown, { theme })` and `orbit render --theme` resolve every property to a plain color, so exported files look the same anywhere. In the browser, `renderer.toSVGString()` also picks up the custom properties your page sets. Background patterns are CSS, so exports keep the `--orbit-surface` color without them.

---

<!-- docs/extending.md -->

# Extending Orbit

Orbit has four ways to make maps your own: **node types**, **actions**, **status words** and **themes**. Each works for one map, through its options, or for every map once registered, which also covers `<orbit-map>` elements and maps in markdown pages, where you don't write code per map. A map's own options win over registered ones.

| | For one map | For every map |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node types | `nodeTypes: { milestone: { … } }` | `registerNodeType('milestone', { … })` |
| Actions | `actions: [{ id, label, run }]` | `registerAction({ id, label, run })` |
| Status words | `statuses: { review: 'active' }` | `registerStatus('review', 'active')` |
| Themes | `theme: { preset, tokens }` | `registerTheme('brand', { preset, tokens })` |

Each `register…` function returns a function that removes the registration again.

## Node types

A node picks a type with the `type` attribute, in any case:

```markdown
# Launch
## v1.0 beta <!-- orbit type: milestone -->
- Ana Torres <!-- orbit type: person, role: Design -->
```

In YAML it's `type: milestone`. The type decides how those nodes look and behave:

```js
import { createOrbitMap } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  nodeTypes: {
    milestone: {
      label: 'Milestone',
      icon: '🏁',
      color: '#F59E0B',
      tokens: { 'node-stroke': '#B45309', 'node-stroke-width': '3' },
    },
    person: {
      label: 'Person',
      render(node, element) {
        element.textContent = node.text.split(' ').map((word) => word[0]).join('');
      },
      details(node, element) {
        element.textContent = `Role: ${node.attrs?.role ?? 'not set'}`;
      },
      actions: [{ id: 'email', label: 'Email', icon: '✉️', run: (node) => window.open(`mailto:${node.attrs?.email}`) }],
    },
  },
});
```

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `label` | The type's name for people, shown as a chip in the detail sheet, in the tooltip and to screen readers. |
| `icon` | The icon these nodes get unless they set their own. |
| `color` | The color these nodes get unless they set their own. Their children take shades of it. |
| `tokens` | [Theme tokens](theming.md#custom-properties) for these nodes only, without `--orbit-`: their rim, shadow, glow, label and status colors. |
| `render(node, element)` | Draws inside the node, the way a picture does. `element` is a 100 × 100 px box, clipped to the node's circle and scaled with it, and the label moves outside, onto a pill that shows the node's icon before its name. Return a function to clean up; it runs when the node leaves the map. |
| `details(node, element)` | Adds a section to the detail sheet, above the note. These nodes get a "Show details" button. |
| `actions` | Actions only these nodes offer, after the map's own. |
| `version` | The version of the fields these nodes keep in their attributes, once the type changes them (1 at first). See [Versions](#versions). |
| `upgrade(node, from)` | Brings a node written for an older version of the type up to date. |

- **Custom attributes** like `<!-- orbit role: Design -->` are on `node.attrs`, which makes them handy in `render` and `details`.
- **`render` is for showing:** clicks go through to the node, so use actions for anything to press. It runs when the node comes on the map; navigating away and back draws it again.
- **Errors stay contained:** if a type's `render` or `details`, or an action, throws, the console says which one and the map keeps working.

### Types for display only

`nodeTypeFor(node)` gives a node that names no type one to be drawn as, as if it said `type: name`: that type's look, what it draws inside and its actions. It's for display only: Orbit never writes it to the map, so saving keeps the node as it was, and never upgrades a node for it.

```js
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  nodeTypes: { progress: { label: 'Progress', render: drawProgressRing } },
  // Ideas with to-dos right under them show a ring, unless they have a type of their own.
  nodeTypeFor: (node) => (node.children.some((child) => child.status) ? 'progress' : undefined),
});
```

- **A node's own `type` wins:** `nodeTypeFor` is only asked about nodes without one.
- **It's asked whenever the map draws,** often, so keep it quick, and return `undefined` to draw a node as it is. An answer that changes with the map, after an edit to the node's children say, shows as the map draws the edit; after a change elsewhere that answers depend on, `render()` the map again.
- **The type shows wherever a type does:** in the detail sheet's chip, the tooltip, what screen readers hear, `data-orbit-type`, the label's font and exports (`renderToSVGString(source, { nodeTypes, nodeTypeFor })`).
- **If it throws,** the console says so once, and nodes are drawn as they are.

### Versions

A type's nodes keep their own fields in attributes, so changing those fields changes what older maps say. Give the type a `version` and an `upgrade` that brings older nodes up to date:

```js
registerNodeType('task', {
  label: 'Task',
  version: 2,
  // Version 1 kept the person in `assignee`; version 2 calls it `owner`.
  upgrade(node, from) {
    if (from < 2 && node.attrs?.assignee !== undefined) {
      const { assignee, ...rest } = node.attrs;
      node.attrs = { ...rest, owner: assignee };
    }
  },
});
```

- **Nodes say which version they were written for:** `type: task@2`; none means 1. A map upgrades older nodes when it draws them, and the next save writes them as `task@2` with their new fields, changing nothing else in the file.
- **Nodes written for a newer version** than the type knows are left as they are, and saving keeps everything in them.
- **Without a map** (on a server, in a script), `upgradeNodeTypes(document.root, nodeTypes)` does the same, with the types you pass and the registered ones, and returns how many nodes it upgraded.
- **If `upgrade` throws,** the console says which type failed and the node stays as it was.

## Actions

Actions are buttons under the node in focus, after Orbit's own (details, picture, video, note, link), and in the node's detail sheet.

```js
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  actions: [
    {
      id: 'assign',
      label: 'Assign',
      icon: '👤',
      when: (node) => node.children.length === 0,
      run: (node, event) => openAssignDialog(node),
    },
  ],
});
```

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The action's name in the `action` event. Use ids other than Orbit's own: `details`, `image`, `video`, `embed`, `note` and `link`. |
| `label` | The button's name, read by screen readers, shown as its tooltip and in the detail sheet. A function gets the node: ``(node) => `Assign ${node.text}` ``. |
| `icon` | An emoji or short symbol (`'✏️'`), SVG path data on a 24-unit grid (`'M4 20h4L20 8l-4-4L4 16z'`), or one of Orbit's icons: `note`, `link`, `goto`, `info`, `image`, `video`, `embed`, `list`. Without one, the label's first letter. |
| `when(node)` | Which nodes offer it. Default: every node. |
| `run(node, event)` | What it does. |

- **The `action` event fires first** (`orbit-action` on the element), with `action` set to the id. `preventDefault()` there, or returning `false` from `onAction`, skips `run`.
- **In the detail sheet,** pressing an action closes the sheet first, so a dialog your action opens is in front.
- **One button per id:** a map's own action wins over a registered one with the same id, and a node type's actions come last.

## Status words

`status` is free text, and [some words](format.md#statuses) get a colored dot. Add your own words, as one of the tones or with a color of their own:

```js
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  statuses: {
    review: 'active',
    shipped: 'done',
    'on hold': '#A855F7',
  },
});
```

The tones are `active`, `done`, `blocked`, `todo` and `neutral`; their colors come from the theme (`--orbit-status-active`, …). Words match in any case.

## Themes

Register a theme once to use it by name everywhere: in options, in a document's frontmatter and on `<orbit-map theme="…">`.

```js
import { registerTheme } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

registerTheme('brand', {
  preset: 'night',
  tokens: { 'color-root': '#FFD166', 'color-1': '#06D6A0', surface: '#0B1020' },
});
```

```markdown
---
theme: brand
---
# Launch
```

- **What a theme is:** it starts from `preset` (a built-in theme or another registered one) and sets its own [tokens](theming.md#custom-properties).
- **Building on it:** a theme object can start from a registered theme too. `{ preset: 'brand', tokens: { … } }` adds its tokens to brand's.
- **Names:** built-in names can't be reused, and `themeNames()` lists every name.
- **Validation:** `orbit validate` doesn't know the themes your code registers, so it reports `theme: brand` as unknown.

## For every map

Register at startup, before maps are created. Maps created earlier pick up registered types, actions and words when they next redraw.

```js
import { defineOrbitMapElement, registerAction, registerNodeType, registerStatus, registerTheme } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

registerTheme('brand', { preset: 'night', tokens: { 'color-root': '#FFD166' } });
registerNodeType('milestone', { label: 'Milestone', icon: '🏁', color: '#F59E0B' });
registerStatus('review', 'active');
registerAction({ id: 'copy-link', label: 'Copy link', icon: 'link', run: (node) => navigator.clipboard.writeText(`${location.href}#${node.id}`) });
defineOrbitMapElement();
```

```html
<orbit-map theme="brand">
# Launch
## v1.0 beta <!-- orbit type: milestone, status: review -->
</orbit-map>
```

The functions they return remove the registrations again, which helps with hot reloading and tests.

## In React

`<OrbitMindMap>` takes the same options as props. Inline objects are fine: the map compares what node types and actions declare, and calls their latest functions, `nodeTypeFor`'s too.

```tsx
import { OrbitMindMap } from '@restless-dreams/orbit/react';

export const Roadmap = ({ markdown, onAssign }: { markdown: string; onAssign: (id: string) => void }) => {
  return (
    <div style={{ height: 480 }}>
      <OrbitMindMap
        source={markdown}
        nodeTypes={{ milestone: { label: 'Milestone', icon: '🏁', color: '#F59E0B' } }}
        actions={[{ id: 'assign', label: 'Assign', icon: '👤', run: (node) => onAssign(node.id) }]}
        statuses={{ review: 'active' }}
      />
    </div>
  );
};
```

## Styling nodes with CSS

Each node's element and label carry hooks for CSS:
- `data-orbit-type`: the type, lowercase;
- `data-orbit-status`: the status word, lowercase;
- `data-orbit-tags`: the tags, separated by spaces.

Page CSS can target these on maps drawn with `createOrbitMap` or React:

```css
.orbit-node[data-orbit-type='milestone'] .orbit-node__shade {
  stroke-dasharray: 4 3;
}

.orbit-label[data-orbit-tags~='urgent'] {
  font-weight: 800;
}
```

A map inside `<orbit-map>` sits in a shadow root that page CSS can't reach, so use a type's `tokens` there.

## Exports

`toSVGString()`, `renderToSVGString()` and `orbit render` draw node types' icons, colors and tokens, and your status colors. `renderToSVGString(source, { nodeTypes, statuses, nodeTypeFor })` takes them as options too. What `render` draws is HTML, so it isn't part of an exported SVG.

---

<!-- docs/editing.md -->

# Editing on the map

People can build a map on the map itself. A **+** in the orbit adds an idea, typed right inside its new planet, a node's text is edited where it is, and a node is dragged to wherever it should go. Each edit animates into place, and the map comes back as orbit-md to save.

## Turn it on

```js
import { createOrbitMap } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  editable: true,
  onEdit: () => save(map.toMarkdown()),
});
```

With `editable`:

- **A + in the orbit.** In focus mode, the orbit keeps a free place after the planets, drawn as a dashed planet with a plus.
  - Press it and type: the text goes inside the new planet.
  - Enter adds the idea right where it was typed and opens the next one after it, so ideas go in one after another, the keyboard staying up.
  - Escape, or Enter with nothing typed, stops.
- **Text edited where it is.** A long press, a right click or F2 on a node turns its label into a field.
  - Enter saves, and Escape leaves the text as it was. Tapping anywhere else saves.
  - A moon flies into its planet's orbit first, so its text has room. In the overview, small nodes get a field floating over them, at a size you can read.
- **Nodes dragged somewhere else** (see [Dragging nodes](#dragging-nodes)).

`<orbit-map editable>` and `<OrbitMindMap editable>` turn it on too.

## Your own menu

To offer more than editing text, show your own menu when a node is long-pressed, right-clicked, or chosen with the context menu key:

```js
const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  editable: true,
  onNodeContext: ({ node, x, y }) => showMenu(x, y, [
    { label: 'Rename', run: () => map.editNode(node.id) },
    { label: 'Add an idea under it', run: () => map.editNewNode(node.id) },
    { label: 'Mark done', run: () => map.updateNode(node.id, { status: 'done' }) },
    { label: 'Delete', run: () => map.removeNode(node.id) },
  ]),
  onEdit: () => save(map.toMarkdown()),
});
```

- **What `node-context` reports:** a long press (half a second, held still; `longPressDelay` changes it) with a finger or a pen, a right click, or the context menu key or Shift+F10 on the node with keyboard focus. `x` and `y` are where to put your menu, in CSS pixels from the map's top left corner: the press, or the node's center for the keyboard.
- **The press is yours** with an `onNodeContext` callback or a `node-context` listener (`map.on('node-context', …)`). It doesn't open the node, it doesn't start editing the text, and the browser's own menu stays closed. A listener for the `orbit-node-context` DOM event takes it by calling `event.preventDefault()`.
- **Without any of them,** a long press edits the text on an editable map, once it's let go without moving: moving it drags the node instead. On other maps, it is an ordinary tap and a right click opens the browser's menu.
- **The same long press can drag the node.** Your menu opens as the press is held; if the finger then moves, `node-drag` fires with `phase: 'start'`, and that's the moment to close the menu: the node is on its way somewhere else.

## Dragging nodes

On an editable map, a node held still lifts: a long press with a finger or a pen, or the mouse held down half a second. Move it, and it follows the press, its moons with it.

- **Onto another node:** that node grows and takes a ring. Let go, and the dragged node goes into it, after its last child.
- **Along the orbit:** a planet keeps its place held, an empty ring where it was, so nothing slides under the finger. Carried along the ring, the place moves as it passes each planet, and the others make room. A planet catches a drop only near its middle; over its rim, the press is on the orbit, placing the node beside it. A moon or a deeper node carried to the orbit takes the + as its place.
- **Let go anywhere else,** and it lands in the place held for it. One that never left its place goes back down. Escape, or a second finger, puts it back.
- **What can't happen:** a node can't go inside itself or anything under it, the sun and the root don't lift, and a map that isn't editable never lifts a node.

Each drop is a `moveNode`: it fires `edit` with `kind: 'move'`, the node flies from where it was let go to its place, and Orbit announces it. A mouse that's let go without moving still clicks, so a slow click opens the node as usual.

```js
const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  editable: true,
  onNodeContext: ({ node, x, y }) => showMenu(x, y, node),
  onNodeDrag: ({ phase }) => {
    if (phase === 'start') {
      closeMenu();
    }
  },
  onEdit: () => save(map.toMarkdown()),
});
```

`node-drag` reports each step: `start` as the node leaves its place (with where it was), `over` whenever where it would go changes (`parent` and `index`, or `null` over no place, for haptics or a hint), and `end` when it's let go (where it went, after the `edit`; `null` when it went back).

## Keys for editing

With `editingKeys` as well as `editable`, the keyboard builds a map the way mind-map apps do:

```js
const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, { editable: true, editingKeys: true });
```

| Key | On a node with keyboard focus | While typing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tab | Adds an idea under it (Insert does too) | Keeps what was typed and goes on under it. With nothing typed, moves the field under the idea before. |
| Shift+Tab | Leaves the map, as usual | Keeps what was typed and goes on a level up, beside the parent |
| Shift+Enter | Adds an idea beside it, right after it | |
| Enter | Flies into it, as without the keys | Keeps what was typed and goes on beside it |
| Delete | Removes it, with everything under it | |

- **A whole map without the mouse:** Tab on the sun and type. Enter brings the next idea, Tab goes under the one just typed, Shift+Tab comes back up, and Escape stops.
- **Tab stays in the map.** Without the keys the map is one tab stop, and Tab leaves it. With them, Tab on a node adds an idea, and Shift+Tab leaves. Turn them on where the map is the page's main tool, such as an editor, rather than for a map among other controls.
- **After Delete,** keyboard focus moves on to the node after the removed one, or the one before it, or its parent. The root stays. To offer undo, keep the markdown from before each edit (see [Saving](#saving)).

## The editing methods

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `editNode(id)` | Opens the field over a node, to type its text where it is. |
| `editNewNode(parentId?, index?)` | Opens the field in the orbit of `parentId` (default: the node in focus), at `index` among its children (default: after the last). It flies there first. |
| `stopEditing(save?)` | Closes the field, keeping what was typed unless `save` is false. |
| `addNode(parentId, { text, …, children }, index?)` | Adds a node under `parentId`, at `index` among its children (default: last), with the nodes `children` lists under it, as many levels down as you like. Returns the new node. |
| `updateNode(id, changes)` | Changes text and attributes: `{ text: 'Budget' }`, `{ status: 'done', color: '#E8A33D' }`. `undefined` removes one: `{ color: undefined }`. Returns the node. |
| `removeNode(id)` | Removes a node and everything under it. The root stays. Returns the removed node. |
| `moveNode(id, parentId, index?)` | Moves a node, with everything under it, under `parentId` at `index`. Under the same parent, it changes the order. Returns the node. |
| `getDocument()` | The map as a document: its tree, and the options its frontmatter set. |
| `toMarkdown()` | The map as orbit-md, frontmatter included. |

To let a language model make these changes, see [Map tools for AI](map-tools.md).

`editNode` and `editNewNode` return false, and the others `null`, when there's nothing to do: an id that isn't in the map, removing or moving the root, or moving a node inside itself. They work on any interactive map. `editable` adds the ways people edit by themselves: the +, editing on a long press, a right click, the context menu key or F2, and dragging.

Besides `text`, `addNode` and `updateNode` take the node's attributes: `icon`, `color`, `status`, `priority`, `tags`, `collapsed`, `type`, `link`, `note`, `noteFormat`, `image`, `video`, `embed`, and `attrs` for your own.

- **Ids come from the text,** as when a map is read from markdown: "Night markets" is `night-markets`, and a second "Ideas" is `ideas-2`. New text gives a node a new id, so the saved file needs no `id` attribute. A node keeps its id when a `#id` link points at it, or when the id was set by hand. Read a node's current id from what the method returns.
- **Titles are one line:** line breaks become spaces, typed or pasted.
- **The reader keeps their place.** When the node in focus, or a node above it, is removed, the nearest node left takes the focus and `focus-change` fires. A node in focus that gets a new id stays in focus.
- **Edits change the tree in place:** `getDocument().root`, which is the tree you passed to `render()` if you passed one.

## Events

| Event | DOM event | Option | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `edit` | `orbit-edit` | `onEdit` | `{ kind, node, tree }`: `kind` is `add`, `update`, `remove` or `move` |
| `editor-open` | `orbit-editor-open` | `onEditorOpen` | `{ node, parent }`: the node whose text is typed, or `node: null` and the `parent` of a new idea |
| `editor-close` | `orbit-editor-close` | `onEditorClose` | the same |
| `node-context` | `orbit-node-context` | `onNodeContext` | `{ node, x, y }` |
| `node-drag` | `orbit-node-drag` | `onNodeDrag` | `{ phase, node, parent, index }`: `phase` is `start`, `over` or `end` |

The field's events help a page around the map: hide a button that would cover the keyboard, say, or bring a phone's keyboard up when an app opens the field itself.

## Saving

Save the map on every `edit`:

```js
map.on('edit', () => localStorage.setItem('map', map.toMarkdown()));
```

- **`toMarkdown()` reads back as the same map,** ids included, and keeps the file as it was written: only the ideas an edit changed are written again, so a note written by hand or by another app keeps its formatting and everything Orbit doesn't read (see [What saving keeps](format.md#what-saving-keeps)). New ideas are written the way people write maps: headings for the root and its children, lists below them, checkboxes for statuses, hashtags for tags. For YAML, use `serializeOrbitYAML(map.getDocument())`.
- **A map written for a newer version of the format** has an `unsupported-schema-version` diagnostic: open it without `editable`, so nothing is changed that this version doesn't understand.
- **Drawing the saved text again is fine.** When `render()` gets the map as it already is, Orbit keeps the view, and an edit's animation carries on.
- **Undo is yours to keep:** save the markdown before an edit, and `render()` it to go back. Orbit animates to the restored map and keeps the reader's place.

## In React

`<OrbitMindMap>` takes `editable`, `onEdit`, `onNodeContext`, `onNodeDrag`, `onEditorOpen` and `onEditorClose`, and the ref's `renderer` has the methods:

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { OrbitMindMap, type OrbitMindMapRef } from '@restless-dreams/orbit/react';

export const Brainstorm = ({ initial }: { initial: string }) => {
  const map = useRef<OrbitMindMapRef>(null);
  const [source, setSource] = useState(initial);
  return (
    <div style={{ height: 480 }}>
      <OrbitMindMap
        ref={map}
        source={source}
        editable
        onEdit={() => setSource(map.current?.renderer?.toMarkdown() ?? source)}
      />
    </div>
  );
};
```

Setting `source` to what the map just wrote doesn't draw it again.

## In `<orbit-map>`

```html
<orbit-map editable>
# Weekend in Lisbon
## Food
## Places
</orbit-map>
```

The element's `renderer` has the same methods, and its events bubble out of it: listen for `orbit-edit` and save `element.renderer.toMarkdown()`. Edits change the map, not the element's text. `<orbit-map editable editing-keys>` turns on the [keys for editing](#keys-for-editing) too.

## Keyboard and screen readers

- **F2** edits the text of the node with keyboard focus. With `editingKeys`, Tab, Shift+Enter and Delete add and remove ideas too (see [Keys for editing](#keys-for-editing)).
- **The +** takes its turn among the planets with `←` and `→`; Enter or Space on it adds an idea.
- **The context menu key** and Shift+F10 open your menu for the node with keyboard focus, so whatever a long press offers works from the keyboard too.
- **The field** is named after what it's for ("Text of Food", "New idea for Trip"), and when it closes with Enter or Escape, keyboard focus returns to the node, or to the +.
- **Announcements:** Orbit announces added, removed and moved nodes in its live region ("Added Night markets").
- **Moving without dragging:** dragging needs a pointer, so offer a way to move nodes in your menu too, with `moveNode` (earlier, later, in, out), as the keyboard can reach it.

---

<!-- docs/map-tools.md -->

# Map tools for AI

Map tools let a language model read a map and change it: add ideas and whole branches, rename them, mark them done, move, sort and remove them. They come in the shape each provider's API takes, so an app can offer an assistant with whichever model its people choose. They work on a map on screen, where every change animates into place, or on a document on a server. A call a model gets wrong changes nothing, and its result says what to send instead.

## Add an assistant to a map

`createMapTools(map)` gives the tools for one map. `tools.for(provider)` lists them for the model, and `tools.run(name, input)` carries out each call it makes. With Anthropic's API:

```js
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { createOrbitMap, createMapTools } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, { onEdit: () => save(map.toMarkdown()) });
const tools = createMapTools(map);
const client = new Anthropic({ apiKey });

const ask = async (request) => {
  const messages = [{ role: 'user', content: request }];

  while (true) {
    const response = await client.messages.create({ model, max_tokens: 4096, system: tools.instructions, tools: tools.for('anthropic'), messages });
    messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: response.content });
    const calls = response.content.filter((block) => block.type === 'tool_use');

    if (calls.length === 0) {
      return response.content.find((block) => block.type === 'text')?.text;
    }

    messages.push({
      role: 'user',
      content: calls.map((call) => {
        const result = tools.run(call.name, call.input);
        return { type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: call.id, content: result.text, is_error: !result.ok };
      }),
    });
  }
};

await ask('Add three day trips from Kyoto, each with a one-sentence note');
```

The map changes as the model works: each new idea flies out of its parent, and `edit` fires for each change, so the map saves as it does when people edit it. Keep API keys off public pages: call the model from your server, or let each person bring their own key.

## Other providers

**OpenAI's Responses API:**

```js
const input = [{ role: 'user', content: request }];

while (true) {
  const response = await openai.responses.create({ model, instructions: tools.instructions, tools: tools.for('openai'), input });
  const calls = response.output.filter((item) => item.type === 'function_call');

  if (calls.length === 0) {
    return response.output_text;
  }

  input.push(...response.output);

  for (const call of calls) {
    input.push({ type: 'function_call_output', call_id: call.call_id, output: tools.run(call.name, call.arguments).text });
  }
}
```

`run` takes the arguments as OpenAI sends them, as JSON text. The tools are written without strict mode, which would make the model send every field of every call.

**Chat Completions,** which most other providers and local servers (OpenRouter, Ollama and many more) offer as well as OpenAI:

```js
const messages = [{ role: 'system', content: tools.instructions }, { role: 'user', content: request }];

while (true) {
  const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model, messages, tools: tools.for('openai-chat') });
  const message = response.choices[0].message;
  messages.push(message);

  if (!message.tool_calls?.length) {
    return message.content;
  }

  for (const call of message.tool_calls) {
    messages.push({ role: 'tool', tool_call_id: call.id, content: tools.run(call.function.name, call.function.arguments).text });
  }
}
```

**Gemini,** with `@google/genai`:

```js
const contents = [{ role: 'user', parts: [{ text: request }] }];

while (true) {
  const response = await ai.models.generateContent({ model, contents, config: { systemInstruction: tools.instructions, tools: tools.for('gemini') } });
  const calls = response.functionCalls ?? [];

  if (calls.length === 0) {
    return response.text;
  }

  contents.push(response.candidates[0].content);
  contents.push({
    role: 'user',
    parts: calls.map((call) => {
      const result = tools.run(call.name, call.args);
      return { functionResponse: { name: call.name, response: result.ok ? { output: result.text } : { error: result.text } } };
    }),
  });
}
```

**MCP:** `tools.definitions` are tools as MCP lists them (`name`, `description`, `inputSchema` and `annotations`). A server returns them for `tools/list`, and answers `tools/call` with `{ content: [{ type: 'text', text: result.text }], isError: !result.ok }`.

For anything else, such as the Vercel AI SDK or LangChain, build the tools from `tools.definitions`: each has a name, a description, and its input as JSON Schema.

## The tools

| Tool | What it does | Takes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_map` | The map as an outline: each node's title, id and attributes, and the start of its note. A big map is cut short, whole levels first, with what's left out counted. | `node_id` (to read one branch), `depth` |
| `find_nodes` | Searches titles, notes and tags, in any case and with or without accents, and statuses by what they mean: `done` finds `shipped` too. | `query`, `status`, `tag` |
| `read_node` | Everything about one node: its whole note, its picture, video or page, where it is, its children, and the nodes that link to it. | `node_id` |
| `add_nodes` | Adds nodes, or whole branches, written as a markdown list. | `parent_id`, `outline`, `index` |
| `update_node` | Changes a title or attributes, and `clear` removes attributes. | `node_id`, `text`, `note`, `status`, `priority`, `tags`, `icon`, `color`, `link`, `image`, `video`, `embed`, `collapsed`, `clear` |
| `move_node` | Moves a branch under another node, or to another place among its siblings. | `node_id`, `parent_id`, `index` |
| `reorder_children` | Puts all the children of a node in a new order at once: to sort them, or to group them. | `parent_id`, `order` |
| `remove_node` | Removes a branch. Never the root. | `node_id` |
| `show_node` | Flies the map to a node. Only on a map on screen. | `node_id` |

New ideas come as orbit-md, the way models write any outline: each list item is a node, the items indented under it are its children, at any depth, and indented text that isn't an item is its note. Checkboxes, an emoji first, hashtags at the end and `<!-- orbit … -->` comments set statuses, icons, tags and other attributes, as in any map:

```json
{
  "parent_id": "marketing",
  "outline": "- Social media\n  - [ ] Instagram #social\n  - TikTok\n- Newsletter\n  A weekly email with what shipped."
}
```

## What a call returns

`run` returns `{ ok, text, changed }`:

- **`text`** is for the model: send it back as the tool's result. It names nodes with their ids (`"Instagram" #instagram`), gives the new id when a new title changes one, and adds notes worth knowing, such as an id the model wrote as a title, a field the tool doesn't take, or two ideas with the same title side by side.
- **`ok`** is false when the call couldn't be carried out. Nothing changed, and `text` says why and what to send instead:

```text
No node has the id "lanch". Did you mean "Launch" #launch? read_map and find_nodes give every node's id.

"Build" #build can't go under "Frontend" #frontend, which is inside it. Move "Frontend" #frontend out of it first, or choose another parent. Nothing changed.

outline doesn't read cleanly. Fix this, and send it again:
- Line 2: Unknown attribute "colour". Did you mean "color"?
Lines count from the outline's first line. Nothing changed.
```

- **`changed`** says whether the map changed.

`run` never throws over a call a model gets wrong. It forgives what models often send: input as JSON text, `null` for a field left out, a number as text, tags as words separated by commas, an id with its `#`, a title only one node has instead of its id, and a field under the name models often give it (`title` for `text`, `parent` for `parent_id`). An id from before a rename still finds its node, and the id of a removed node says it was removed. A misspelled field, or a value the map can't use, changes nothing and says what it takes.

## On screen, or on a server

- **A map on screen:** `createMapTools(map)` takes what `createOrbitMap` returns, the `renderer` of an `<orbit-map>` element, or the `renderer` of `OrbitMindMap`'s ref. Each change goes through `addNode`, `updateNode`, `moveNode` and `removeNode` (see [Editing](editing.md)): it animates, Orbit announces it, and `edit` fires. `read_map` says which node the reader is looking at, and `show_node` takes them to one.
- **A document:** `createMapTools(markdown)` or `createMapTools(parseOrbit(markdown))`, on a server or anywhere without a map on screen. The tools change the document in place, and `serializeOrbitMarkdown(tools.document)` saves it, the way it was written apart from what changed.

```js
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { createMapTools, serializeOrbitMarkdown } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

const tools = createMapTools(markdown);
tools.run('add_nodes', { parent_id: 'research', outline: '- Interviews\n- Survey' });
await writeFile('map.md', serializeOrbitMarkdown(tools.document));
```

Options:

- **`readOnly: true`** offers only the tools that read (and `show_node`, on screen): for an assistant that answers questions about a map.
- **`readLimit`**: the most nodes `read_map` shows at once. Default 250.

## Good to know

- **Instructions.** `tools.instructions` says how to use the tools, and asks for short titles with the detail in notes, ideas in the map's language, and nodes removed only when asked: put it in the system prompt. To save the model a first call, put `tools.run('read_map').text` in the first message too.
- **Undo.** Keep `map.toMarkdown()` from before a request: `map.render(saved)` puts the map back, animating to it.
- **Asking first.** Each definition's `annotations` say whether the tool only reads (`readOnlyHint`) and whether it can overwrite or remove something (`destructiveHint`). An app can run the tools that read at once and ask before the others, as MCP clients do.
- **Schemas every provider reads.** The inputs use plain JSON Schema, without references or unions, and new branches come as markdown rather than nested objects, which some providers' schemas can't describe.
- **Newer maps.** A map written for a newer version of the format can be read but not changed, so nothing this version doesn't understand is lost.

---

<!-- docs/media.md -->

# Pictures and videos

A node's picture shows inside its planet, and a video shows its thumbnail with a play badge ([Media](format.md#media) has how to write them). Under the node in focus, "View image" and "Play video" open them in the media viewer, over the whole window.

- [The media viewer](#the-media-viewer)
- [Keys](#keys)
- [Choosing what the buttons do](#choosing-what-the-buttons-do)
- [From code](#from-code)
- [Events](#events)
- [YouTube and Vimeo](#youtube-and-vimeo)
- [Sound and autoplay](#sound-and-autoplay)
- [Maps that aren't interactive](#maps-that-arent-interactive)
- [Looks](#looks)

## The media viewer

The viewer covers the whole window, even when the map sits in a small box on a page, and follows the map's theme, light or dark.

- **Pictures** fit the window, never past twice their own size. The wheel, a pinch, a double click or tap, the `+`, `−` and `0` keys and the zoom buttons zoom around the point under the pointer or between the fingers, and a zoomed picture pans with a drag. Zooming goes to four times the fitted size, or until the picture shows at twice its own size if that's further.
- **Videos** start at once: files (`.mp4`, `.webm`, `.mov`) in the browser's own player, YouTube and Vimeo in theirs. The player is as big as the window allows, at the video's shape once it's known (16:9 until then, upright for YouTube Shorts). Stepping away from a video stops it.
- **Every picture and video of the map,** in reading order (the order the outline lists the map, a node's picture before its video): the previous and next buttons, the arrow keys and, on touch screens, a swipe step through them, starting from the one opened. A counter says where you are ("2 of 5"), and screen readers hear it.
- **Around them,** the node's title, the caption, and the picture's description (its alt text, which is also the picture's name for screen readers), with a link to open the picture on its own, or the video on its site.
- **Closing:** Esc, the close button, a click around the media or, on touch screens, a swipe down while the picture isn't zoomed. Focus goes back where it was, and the map's own keys, which rest while the viewer is open, work again.

The detail sheet shows a node's picture and video too. Its picture opens the viewer, over the sheet, and its video has an Expand button that moves it there (a video file goes on from where it was); closing the viewer goes back to the sheet.

## Keys

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `←` `→` | The previous or next picture or video; on a zoomed picture, pan it |
| `↑` `↓` | Pan a zoomed picture |
| `Home` `End` | The first or last picture or video |
| `+` `−` `0` | Zoom in, zoom out, fit the picture to the window |
| `Space` | Play or pause the video |
| `Escape` | Close the viewer |

On a video's own controls, the arrow keys and the space bar are the player's. Inside YouTube's and Vimeo's players every key is theirs, Escape included: Tab out of the player, or click around it, to close the viewer.

## Choosing what the buttons do

The buttons ask your code first, as every button does: `onAction`, then the `action` event. What happens next:

| Your code | "View image" and "Play video" |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing | Open the media viewer |
| `mediaViewer: false` | Open the detail sheet at the picture or video, as before the viewer |
| `mediaViewer: false` and `showDetailSheet: false` | Nothing: Orbit opens neither |
| `showDetailSheet: false` | Open the media viewer: it turns off only the sheet, for notes, embeds and details |
| `onAction` returns `false`, or `preventDefault()` on the `action` event | Nothing: the press is yours |

The detail sheet's picture and Expand button are presses of "View image" and "Play video" too: your code sees them first, and when it takes one the sheet closes, so what you open is in front. With `mediaViewer: false`, the sheet's picture is only a picture.

```js
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, {
  onAction: ({ node, action }) => {
    if (action === 'image') {
      openMyLightbox(node.image.src);
      return false;
    }

    return undefined;
  },
});
```

## From code

A page can open the viewer itself, to show a picture big or play a video on a screen of its own:

```js
map.openMedia('summit');                                    // a node's picture, or its video if it has no picture
map.openMedia('trail', { kind: 'video', autoplay: false }); // its video, ready to play
map.openMedia('trail', { kind: 'video', startAt: 42 });     // its video, playing from 0:42
map.playMedia();
map.seekMedia(42);
map.pauseMedia();
map.unmuteMedia();                                          // from a press: the sound of a video a browser started muted
map.closeMedia();
```

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `openMedia(nodeId, { kind, autoplay, startAt })` | Shows the node's picture (`kind: 'image'`, the default when it has one) or video (`kind: 'video'`), opening the viewer if it's closed. A video starts playing unless `autoplay` is `false`, from its start or `startAt` seconds in (YouTube and Vimeo start at the whole second). Returns `false` when the map has no such node, or the node no such picture or video. |
| `closeMedia()` | Closes the viewer. |
| `playMedia()`, `pauseMedia()` | Plays or pauses the video it shows. Returns `false` when it shows no video it can drive. |
| `seekMedia(seconds)` | Moves the video to `seconds` from its start. Returns `false` when it shows no video it can drive. |
| `unmuteMedia()` | Turns on the sound of the video it shows. Browsers allow it only from a press (see [Sound and autoplay](#sound-and-autoplay)). Returns `false` when it shows no video it can drive. |

`openMedia` opens the viewer whatever `mediaViewer`, `showDetailSheet` and `interactive` say: those choose what the buttons do. Files, YouTube and Vimeo can be driven; a video on any other site plays in a frame, with its own controls only. `<orbit-map>` has the same six methods.

This is what an audience's screen does while someone presents from a phone: it opens what the presenter opens, where the presenter's video is, and follows the presenter's player, and tells the phone how the video is going.

```js
const map = createOrbitMap(element, markdown, { interactive: false, showControls: false });

presenter.addEventListener('message', ({ data }) => {
  if (data.type === 'media') {
    map.openMedia(data.id, { kind: data.kind, autoplay: data.playing, startAt: data.seconds });
  } else if (data.type === 'play') {
    map.playMedia();
  } else if (data.type === 'pause') {
    map.pauseMedia();
  } else if (data.type === 'seek') {
    map.seekMedia(data.seconds);
  } else if (data.type === 'close') {
    map.closeMedia();
  }
});

map.on('media-state', ({ node, playing, time }) => {
  presenter.postMessage({ type: 'state', id: node.id, playing, time });
});
```

## Events

| Event | DOM event | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `media-open` | `orbit-media-open` | `{ node, kind, index, total }`: the viewer opened, or stepped, on a node's picture (`kind: 'image'`) or video (`'video'`), `index` of `total` in reading order, from 0 |
| `media-close` | `orbit-media-close` | `{ node, kind, index, total }`: the viewer closed, showing that |
| `media-state` | `orbit-media-state` | `{ node, playing, time, duration, ended, muted }`: the video started, paused, moved to another time, ended or was muted, at once; while it plays, its time a few times a second. `time` and `duration` are in seconds; `duration` is `null` until it's known |

`onMediaOpen`, `onMediaClose` and `onMediaState` receive the same, and so do the React props of the same names. The DOM events bubble from the map's container and out of `<orbit-map>`.

## YouTube and Vimeo

YouTube videos play in YouTube's privacy-enhanced player (`youtube-nocookie.com`), and Vimeo videos in Vimeo's with `dnt=1`, which tracks no sessions. Links to watch pages, `youtu.be`, Shorts, Vimeo channels, groups, showcases and unlisted videos all work; Orbit frames their players, never their pages, which refuse to be framed.

- **The referrer:** the players' frames send the page's origin, never its address (`referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"`). YouTube's player won't play without knowing the site it's on (its "Error 153"), and a page that sends no referrer (`Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`) still gives its origin to these frames. A page opened from a file has no origin to give, so YouTube's videos don't play there.
- **Driving them:** `playMedia`, `pauseMedia` and `seekMedia` reach the players through the messages their own JavaScript APIs send (YouTube's `enablejsapi=1`, with the page's `origin`; Vimeo's player.js messages), and `media-state` follows what the players say. Nothing is loaded from either site but the player itself.
- **Other sites:** a video on any other site plays in a frame, as the detail sheet shows an embed, with only its own controls: `playMedia` and its kin return `false` for it, and it reports no `media-state`.

## Sound and autoplay

Browsers let a video start with sound only once the reader has interacted with the page. A press of "Play video", the arrows or a swipe counts, so those videos play with sound.

A video opened from code on a page nobody has touched yet, such as an audience's screen, may not be allowed to. A video file then starts muted, and its `media-state` says `muted: true`. YouTube's and Vimeo's players decide for themselves: they start muted, or wait for a press. Screens that should play sound from the start can allow it: a kiosk Chrome with `--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required`, or an Android `WebView` with `setMediaPlaybackRequiresUserGesture(false)`.

Elsewhere, offer a button for the sound while `media-state` says the video is muted, or isn't playing when it should. Its press counts as interacting with the page, so `unmuteMedia()` and `playMedia()` from its click play the video with sound, YouTube's and Vimeo's included. The viewer is a modal `<dialog>` in the top layer, and a modal dialog makes the rest of the page inert, popovers included: show the button in a `<dialog>` of its own with `showModal()`, after the viewer opens, so it's on top and can be pressed.

```js
soundButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  map.unmuteMedia();
  map.playMedia();
  soundDialog.close();
});
```

## Maps that aren't interactive

On a map with `interactive: false`, a still picture, the viewer is the page's to drive. It shows the picture or video with its title and caption, but no buttons, no counter and no controls on videos, and it takes no input of its own: Esc and clicks don't close it, and keys and presses reach the page, so a presentation's own keys keep working. Open, close and play it with the methods above.

## Looks

The viewer takes its colors from the detail sheet's custom properties: `--orbit-sheet-background` behind the media (blurred by `--orbit-sheet-blur` where it's see-through, as in the glass themes), `--orbit-sheet-text` and `--orbit-sheet-muted-text` for the title, caption and counter, and `--orbit-sheet-shadow` under a video. Its buttons are the map's controls (`--orbit-control-*`, `--orbit-focus-ring`). See [Theming](theming.md#custom-properties).

With reduced motion (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`), zooms and steps happen at once instead of gliding and fading.

---

<!-- docs/languages.md -->

# Languages

Orbit speaks the language of the page it's on: its buttons, the detail sheet, the media viewer, the list of the map, its messages and everything screen readers hear about the map. English and Spanish are built in. You can add any other language, change single words, or pick a language for one map.

Only Orbit's own words change. The text of a map is the author's, and so are the status words written in it (`status: done` shows as "done"). Problems Orbit reports about a map's source (in the console, `orbit validate` and diagnostics) stay in English: they're for the map's author and their tools.

## Which language a map speaks

A map speaks the language of the element it's drawn in: the closest `lang` attribute around it, through shadow roots, and then the page's own `<html lang>`. A page in Spanish gets its maps in Spanish with nothing to set:

```html
<html lang="es">
  …
  <orbit-map># Viaje
## Comida
## Lugares</orbit-map>
```

The `language` option picks a language for one map, whatever the page says:

```ts
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, { language: 'es' });
```

```tsx
<OrbitMindMap source={markdown} language="es" />
```

On `<orbit-map>`, set its `lang` attribute, as on any element: `<orbit-map lang="es">`.

Languages are [BCP 47 tags](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp47). A regional tag speaks its language with the region's numbers and plurals: `es-MX` and `es-ES` both speak Spanish, writing 24,000 and 24.000. A language Orbit doesn't have speaks English, and so does a map on a page that names none.

Changing the language later, with `setOptions({ language })`, the `language` prop or the element's `lang` attribute, writes the map's words again where they are.

## Adding a language

`registerLanguage` adds a language for every map, by its tag. Words it leaves out are English, or, for a regional tag like `pt-BR`, its base language's (`pt`) when Orbit has it:

```ts
import { registerLanguage } from '@restless-dreams/orbit';

registerLanguage('fr', {
  focus: 'Focus',
  overview: 'Vue d’ensemble',
  zoomIn: 'Zoomer',
  zoomOut: 'Dézoomer',
  ideaCount: { one: '{count} idée', many: '{count} d’idées', other: '{count} idées' },
  // …the rest of the words in the table below.
});
```

It returns a function that takes the language away again. Registering a language Orbit already has changes its words for every map: `registerLanguage('es', { video: 'Vídeo' })`. `languageTags()` lists the languages maps can speak.

### Placeholders, plurals and lists

- **Placeholders:** words in braces (`{name}`, `{count}`) are filled in for you. Keep them in a translation, in whatever order the language needs.
- **Plurals:** text with a number is an object of plural forms, one for each [plural category](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/PluralRules/select) the language uses (`zero`, `one`, `two`, `few`, `many`) and `other`, which is required and covers any form left out.
- **Numbers and lists:** numbers are written the way the language writes them, and lists like "has note, image, and link" are joined the language's way ("tiene nota, imagen y enlace").

## Changing single words

The `strings` option changes words on one map, over its language's:

```ts
createOrbitMap(element, markdown, { strings: { zoomIn: 'Closer', zoomOut: 'Further' } });
```

A word Orbit doesn't have, or one of the wrong kind, is skipped with a warning in the console.

## The root Orbit makes up

A map that's just a list, or has several top headings, and has no title gets a root Orbit makes up, named "Untitled map" in the map's language. When you parse maps yourself, `parseOrbit(source, { untitled: 'Mapa sin título' })` gives it that name. Its id is `untitled-map` in every language, so links and saved places keep working, and saving the map writes it as the list it was.

## Without a browser

`renderToSVGString(markdown, { language: 'es' })` writes the drawing's few words in a language: an untitled idea's name, the empty map's message and the map's title when it has none. On the command line: `orbit render map.md --language es`.

<!-- docs/accessibility.md -->

# Accessibility

Orbit maps are built to work with a keyboard, a screen reader, a phone and a preference for less motion.

## Keyboard

The map is one tab stop: Tab moves into the map and out of it again, and the arrow keys move inside it.

| Key | Focus mode | Overview |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `←` `→` | Previous or next planet, and the + on editable maps; the orbit turns so the chosen planet is on top | Previous or next sibling |
| `↓` | From the sun into the orbit | First child |
| `↑` | Back to the sun | Parent |
| `Home` `End` | First or last planet | The root, or the last sibling |
| `Enter` `Space` | Fly into the focused node (on the sun: go back up) | Fly into the focused node |
| `Escape` `Backspace` | Go back up a level | Back to focus mode |
| `+` `−` `0` | Zoom in, zoom out, fit | Zoom in, zoom out, fit |
| `F2` | Edit the focused node's text where it is ([editing](editing.md)) | The same |
| Context menu key, `Shift` `F10` | The map's own menu for the focused node, when the page has one | The same |

The focused node has a visible ring and shows a tooltip with its full text, status and the start of its note. The breadcrumbs, the view switch, the list button, the zoom buttons and the content buttons under the focused node are ordinary buttons, reached with Tab.

In the media viewer, `←` and `→` step through the map's pictures and videos (or pan a zoomed picture), `Home` and `End` go to the first and last, `+`, `−` and `0` zoom a picture, `Space` plays or pauses a video, and `Escape` closes it. Its buttons are ordinary buttons too ([Keys](media.md#keys)).

## Screen readers

- Everything below is said in the map's language: the page's, or the one its `language` option names ([Languages](languages.md)).
- The map is a group named after the document's title (or `ariaLabel`), with the role description "mind map".
- Each node is a button whose name says what it is: its text, its status, how many items it holds and what content it has ("Discovery, 4 items, has note"). The focused node is marked as the current one.
- A visually hidden outline lists the whole map as nested lists, so screen readers can browse every node without moving the map. The list button shows the same outline to everyone.
- Moving around is announced: "Discovery, 4 items", or "Overview of the whole map". So are edits made on the map: "Added Night markets", "Removed Beaches".
- The detail sheet is a modal dialog: focus moves into it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the button that opened it.
- So is the media viewer, named after the node it shows. A picture's description (its alt text) is the picture's name, and also shows under it. The counter ("2 of 5", with the node's title) is read out as you step, and a video's own controls are the browser's or its site's.

## Motion

When the reader asks for reduced motion (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`):

- views cross-fade in place instead of flying;
- a flicked orbit stops where it is let go instead of coasting;
- the orbit's drift (`orbitAnimation`) stays still, and transitions such as the hover lift and the sheet's slide-in are off;
- in the media viewer, zooms and steps happen at once instead of gliding and fading.

`transitionDuration: 0` turns flights off for everyone.

## Reading

- Names inside nodes are never smaller than 9 px on screen, and they keep their size whatever the zoom. A node too small for its name shows none until you zoom in; the outline lists every node, whatever the view.
- Labels meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) in every built-in theme, on every branch color and shade, including where a planet's shading or a translucent planet's background shows through. A test checks this for every theme. Labels use whichever of the theme's dark and light text has more contrast with the node, custom colors included.
- The `contrast` theme is for readers who need more: black outlines and text, bold labels, solid orbits and no shading, with labels above 7:1 (AAA).
- Labels too long for their node show in full in the tooltip and the outline.
- In forced-colors mode (Windows High Contrast), rims and the focus ring use system colors.

## Touch

- Buttons are at least 40 px on touch screens.
- On a page that scrolls, one finger scrolls the page past the map, except on the orbit itself, where it spins the orbit; two fingers zoom.
- A long press on a node opens the page's own menu for it, when the page has one, or edits its text on editable maps; the context menu key, Shift+F10 and F2 do the same from the keyboard.
- The field for typing on the map keeps a 16 px font, scaled to the label's size, so phones don't zoom into it.
- The detail sheet is a bottom sheet you can swipe down to close.
- In the media viewer, two fingers zoom a picture, one pans it once it's zoomed, a swipe across steps to the previous or next picture or video, and a swipe down closes it. On narrow screens, the previous and next buttons sit under a video, clear of its player's controls.

## What authors can do

- Give images alt text: `![The summit at sunrise](summit.jpg)`. It is the picture's name in the media viewer and the detail sheet, and shows under it in the viewer.
- Give the map a title in its frontmatter (`title: Product roadmap`), or pass `ariaLabel`.
- Keep node text short; put details in notes, which are read in full in the detail sheet.
- Prefer statuses (`<!-- orbit status: blocked -->`) over color alone to convey state: statuses are announced and shown as words in the detail sheet.

---

<!-- docs/agents.md -->

# Coding agents

Orbit is built so coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others) can use it correctly on the first try: the whole format and API are in files the package ships, problems come with the fix, and maps can be checked without a browser.

## Give your agent the docs

- **`llms.txt`** is an index of the docs, and **`llms-full.txt`** is all of them in one file: the format, the API, recipes for each framework, theming and accessibility. Both ship in the package (`node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit/llms-full.txt`, matching the installed version) and online for the latest release at `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@restless-dreams/orbit/llms.txt` and `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@restless-dreams/orbit/llms-full.txt`.
- Tell your agent about them in your project's `AGENTS.md`, which Codex, Kimi Code and most other agents read. Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, where a line with `@AGENTS.md` brings in the same file.

```markdown
## Mind maps

This project draws mind maps with Orbit (@restless-dreams/orbit). Before
writing a map or code that uses it, read
node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit/llms-full.txt. Check every map with
`npx @restless-dreams/orbit validate --json <file>` and fix every diagnostic
it lists.
```

## Install the skill

The package includes an agent skill in `skills/orbit`, in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format that Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and other agents read: a `SKILL.md` with instructions they load on their own when a task involves mind maps, and the guides to the format, recipes, theming, extending, editing, pictures and videos, and languages next to it.

The [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) puts it where each agent in your project looks for skills:

```bash
npx skills add restless-dreams/orbit
# From the installed package, so the skill matches its version:
npx skills add ./node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit
# For particular agents (codex, claude-code, kimi-code-cli, cursor, github-copilot…), or with -g for all your projects:
npx skills add ./node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit -a codex -a claude-code -a kimi-code-cli
```

Or copy the folder by hand, to where your agent looks:

| Agent | In a project | For all your projects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex, Kimi Code | `.agents/skills/orbit` | `~/.agents/skills/orbit` |
| Claude Code | `.claude/skills/orbit` | `~/.claude/skills/orbit` |
| Cursor, GitHub Copilot | `.agents/skills/orbit` | their own folders (`npx skills add -g` knows them) |

```bash
mkdir -p .agents/skills && cp -r node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit/skills/orbit .agents/skills/
mkdir -p .claude/skills && cp -r node_modules/@restless-dreams/orbit/skills/orbit .claude/skills/
```

Agents use the skill when a task calls for it, or when you ask for it by name: `$orbit` in Codex, `/orbit` in Claude Code, `/skill:orbit` in Kimi Code.

## What agents can rely on

- **One way to do each thing.** `createOrbitMap(element, markdown, options)` for any page, `<orbit-map>` without a build step, `OrbitMindMap` from `@restless-dreams/orbit/react`, `@restless-dreams/orbit/marked` for markdown pipelines and `renderToSVGString` without a browser.
- **Typed options.** Every option is in the type declarations, and TypeScript rejects one that doesn't exist (plain JavaScript ignores it). A few are spelled their own way where they're set: the frontmatter's `view` is `viewMode` in code and `view-mode` on `<orbit-map>`, and its `animation`, `speed` and `title` are `orbitAnimation`, `orbitSpeed` and `ariaLabel` in code.
- **A starting point.** `npx @restless-dreams/orbit example > map.md` writes a map that shows the main features; `--yaml` writes it as YAML.
- **Problems with the fix.** Parsing is forgiving, and every problem is reported with what to do about it, and with its line wherever it has one: `Unknown frontmatter key "rings" (ignored). Did you mean "showRings"?`, `Unknown theme "dark". Themes: paper, night, … Did you mean "night"?`, `view must be "focus" or "all" (the overview), got "overview".`
- **Checks without a browser.**

```bash
npx @restless-dreams/orbit validate --json map.md
```

```json
{
  "valid": false,
  "flavor": "markdown",
  "root": "Product roadmap",
  "nodes": 22,
  "depth": 3,
  "diagnostics": [
    {
      "code": "unknown-link-target",
      "message": "\"Offline sync\" links to #search-indx, but no node has that id. Did you mean #search-index?",
      "line": 30,
      "severity": "warning"
    }
  ]
}
```

  The command exits with 1 while the map has a problem: fix it and validate again until `valid` is true. Add `--tree` to see the map as Orbit reads it, a node a line with its `#id`: what became a node and what stayed in a note, and the ids that `#id` links and `--focus` take. A few diagnostics only note something and don't make a map invalid: an attribute Orbit doesn't know, kept as one of your own (`unknown-attribute`: often a typo, so read its "Did you mean"), a root Orbit made up for several top-level nodes (`synthetic-root`), a caption with nothing to caption, and an older version of the format, upgraded. `validate` doesn't know what your code registers: it reports a theme of your own as unknown (`--loose` accepts that), and the attributes your node types read as ones it doesn't know, which only notes them. In code, `parseOrbit(source).diagnostics` holds the same list, and `{ strict: true }` throws on the first problem that makes a map invalid.
- **A page to review it.** `npx @restless-dreams/orbit export --html map.md --out map.html` makes one web page with Orbit, the map and its pictures inside. Send it to someone, or to the user's phone, and it opens in any browser, offline, to explore the map or present it.
- **A picture of the result.** `npx @restless-dreams/orbit render map.md --view all --out map.svg` draws the whole map as a standalone SVG. Without `--view all` it draws the map as it opens, centered on the root, where the levels below the root's children have no labels. Open the SVG, or turn it into a PNG with any converter, to look at it.
- **Messages for the usual setup mistakes:** drawing into an element that isn't there throws (`Orbit needs an element to draw the map in, but got null…`), and the console says when the container has no height (`The map has no height, so nothing shows…`) and when a `theme` option, the frontmatter or `<orbit-map theme>` names a theme that doesn't exist.

## Asking for a map

Agents do well with the map's content and where it goes. For example:

- "Turn the outline in NOTES.md into an orbit-md map in docs/roadmap.md and add it to the docs page with `<orbit-map>`. Check it with `orbit validate`."
- "Show our product areas as an Orbit map on the dashboard, in the cosmos theme, with each team's status."
- "Generate a YAML map for Orbit from `teams.json` at build time and render it to SVG for the README."
